body:
I've been doing a little thinking about this the last few days.

Can't we get around the once-per-session requirement by just putting the warning code in `starship init` instead of `starship prompt`? That way the warnings will only fire when running the initialization code (which can afford to be a little slower than the rendering code).

We could also log a setting in the config that tells us how often we want to be warned, and the last time we were warned, e.g.

```
[warnings]
last_warn_time = "2020-04-01 15:00:32 +0600"
warn_interval = "2h"
```
As an added bonus, the user could set the `warn_interval` to "never" or something to indicate that they don't want warnings at all (though including a setting like this might be dangerous--it might be better to allow a maximum warning interval of every 30 days or something).

This won't allow us to do warnings for everything--for example, warning about a segfaulting python interpreter which cannot return version numbers might not be doable under this scheme, but I think most warnings can be handled via a system like this.

I think for anything more sophisticated (per-warning suppression, tracking which warnings have been issued), we would have to add additional persistent data outside of starship.toml, which we *could* do, but my impression is that we've been trying our best to avoid that.

> Can't we get around the once-per-session requirement by just putting the warning code in `starship init` instead of `starship prompt`?

That's a good idea. 🤔
Unfortunately, that would only let us surface errors at startup (e.g. config errors), but none at runtime (e.g. segfaulting python interpreter).

> We could also log a setting in the config that tells us how often we want to be warned

I worry that writing to a user's config file may lead to a separate class of errors. We would need to ensure we have write access to the config file. Users may be version controlling it as part of their dotfiles, so regular updates to the file could be bothersome. 

> I think for anything more sophisticated (per-warning suppression, tracking which warnings have been issued), we would have to add additional persistent data outside of starship.toml, which we could do, but my impression is that we've been trying our best to avoid that.

I think we're starting to reach a point where having persistent data may be needed to allow for greater flexibility and performance improvements:
- Being able to track the created/modified dates and sizes of binaries would allow us to memoize runtime versions
- Being able to track the dirty files in a git repo would allow us to check those files' git statuses first before checking the full repo

I think I agree with your assessment. I think one of the reasons I argued for not going 1.0 last year was because of the need for a change in the observable behaviour of starship when implementing persistent logging and the potential for config file breakage, so I guess it's time to put that to use.

Some more thoughts: someone was arguing for a daemon or background process--do we want to consider that? My vote is for files, since the file abstraction pretty much exists wherever shells do (shells are pretty useless without files), while daemons might not be allowed (e.g. on systems with restricted shells, termux).

If we're going with files, some more questions:
  - How do we synchronize them? Two instances of starship could potentially write to the data file simultaneously, corrupting the data. Do we want to use file locking? (potential speed issues, doesn't protect against other applications writing to the file)
  - What format should we use? Binary is potentially smaller and faster to write, but it'll be a lot harder to debug (and a *lot* harder to debug remotely) if something goes wrong. It's not clear to me how much data we'll be storing--do we want to make this flexible upfront so that we can switch between the two if needed?
  - Where does it go? `~/.config` (on UNIXlikes) seems like the wrong directory.

> Some more thoughts: someone was arguing for a daemon or background process--do we want to consider that? My vote is for files, since the file abstraction pretty much exists wherever shells do (shells are pretty useless without files), while daemons might not be allowed (e.g. on systems with restricted shells, termux).

@nickwb consolidated their thoughts on a daemon implementation, which looks like a good starting point to the daemon discussion: https://gist.github.com/nickwb/b12edea4152414bf5858c7b66f8171fe

I think I'm partial to the file implementation too, but I can be easily swayed. Both have their pros and cons.

> How do we synchronize them?

I think locking would be sensible.
We expect the prompt to render within a few tens/hundreds of ms. If we're running into perf issues because of the locking, I think it's a sign that something else is wrong that would be holding up the prompt.

> What format should we use?

If we add debug commands to serialize and log the contents, it should solve our debugging issue (ofc assuming it works).

> Where does it go?

I was thinking we could start using `~/.starship`, moving `~/.config/starship.toml` to `~/.starship/config.toml`.

I think there's a case to be made for doing file-based stuff first in either case, since the daemon will still need access to persistent data between reboots (e.g. if the user has to log out and back in, or reset the system), and this data will need to be stored/serialized somehow. In the simplest case, we can implement the daemon by doing a little IPC and by turning the on-disk file into an in-memory file.

I think a `~/.starship` directory makes a lot of sense. We could put log file(s) in there, and roll them over every 5MB or so.

For config, we could auto-migrate by copying any `~/.config/starship.toml` to `~/.starship/config.toml` if we detected the first existed but the second did not.

My notes on the daemon which you referred to also talk about some local files for managing exclusive locks and sharing a socket address, so this would be a natural home for those too.

I have made a one-file-per-session store for displaying messages by using a random session key in https://github.com/heyrict/starship/tree/feat/error-module.

Generating a random key requires the `sha256sum` coreutils binary and `/dev/urandom` as a random character generator. I'm not familiar with windows and don't know if there is a workaround there.

![Screenshot from 2020-04-22 20-37-47](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/25698503/79982642-36c6f680-84d9-11ea-8667-baeff2413aac.png)

Oh, I should have joined the discussion before getting down to the implementation.

Here's the answer to @chipbuster 's question in the implementation above.

> How do we synchronize them?

Two different terminals have different files to store the viewed messages.

> What format should we use?

Currently it uses a text file with hash of viewed messages separated by a line break. I think using some keys (e.g. `DEPRECATE_FORMAT_KEY`) when defining a message should be better.

> Where does it go?

/tmp in Linux and mac and C:\Windows\Temp in Windows. Maybe it would be better to use some external libs that provide the path to the temporary directory.

---

I would personally prefer log files be stored in `~/.cache/starship` or `/tmp`. My PC has up to 3 gigabytes of spare disk space most of the time and I always have to clear the useless files e.g. in `~/.cache`. Storing logs in `~/.cache` may not sound so correct but it would be more convenient to clean them when log becomes larger.

I think something like `$XDG_CACHE_DIR` (falling back to the platform-specific cache directories) would be better as well. I don't know about `/tmp` since that's RAM-mounted on some machines (most of my machines), and I don't want to get spammed by warning messages when I reboot.

> Maybe it would be better to use some external libs that provide the path to the temporary directory.

We discussed something like this briefly on #896, but at least for config, it seems there's no satisfying everyone. Kitty had this problem too--no matter which way you set it, someone's going to want it the other way around. Maybe the location could be specified in the starship config, falling back to some platform-specific default? I doubt people will care as much about their data dump location as their config location.
Do you think we should address this issue before format string release? There won't be much breakage as what is designed initially now (as per #1116).
